title: The Reading Is Unclear

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA describes the anomaly as 'a wonderful mystery!' She has run seventeen scans. Each one says something different. She thinks this is exciting!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV's sensors have returned four conflicting readings. He has averaged them. The average is also wrong. He is logging this under 'physics: check again later.'
ai_flavor.rex: REX has weapons locked on the anomaly. He is aware that weapons do not work on phenomena. He is doing it anyway.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's sponsor metrics have gone strange near the anomaly. His last six ad impressions were delivered to coordinates that don't exist. He is unsettled.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that previous ships reported this anomaly and then filed incomplete follow-up reports. She'd have read those before flying any closer. But you're the captain.

body:
The sensors disagree.

The object ahead registers as a spatial distortion, a dense mineral body, a defunct communications array, and — on one reading, briefly — a very large plant.

The ship computer cannot reconcile the data. It has flagged the situation as 'anomalous,' which is its way of saying it also does not know what is happening.

choices.text: Scan thoroughly — take readings from all arrays

outcome.narrative: The gas analyzer resolves the readings. The anomaly is a dense pocket of exotic matter wrapped in a refractive field — genuinely unusual, scientifically interesting, and completely harmless. You collect a sample. The ship computer updates its 'physics: check again later' file to 'physics: noted, moving on.'

choices.text: Send a probe — see what comes back

outcome.narrative: The probe returns. It has collected something. The something registers as exotic matter on three of the four sensor arrays. The fourth sensor array is now humming a frequency it has never produced before. The ship computer has muted it.

choices.text: Navigate around it — some readings are best left unread

outcome.narrative: You took the long way around. The readings normalized once you were past it. The ship computer closed the anomaly file without a summary. This is the first time it has done that.

choices.text: Fly straight through — the sensors are probably wrong

outcome.narrative: You flew through it. Nothing happened. The sensors are still disagreeing. The ship computer has added a note to the navigation log: 'Unknown. Passed through. Fine. Probably.' The 'probably' is doing a lot of work.

title: Something Answered

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA received the signal! She isn't sure what it said! She sent a greeting back! She feels this was the right choice! She is now less sure!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has analyzed the signal. It is not a natural phenomenon. It is also not in any known communication protocol. He is filing this under 'problems for future MARV.'
ai_flavor.rex: REX has weapons locked. He would like to shoot the signal. He understands that you cannot shoot a signal. He would like to try.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP received the signal on his brand frequency. He attempted to serve an advertisement. The signal did not respond to the advertisement. Nothing has responded to an advertisement like this before.
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that the signal appears to be a response to your approach. Which means it was waiting. She did suggest a wider berth, but sure, let's say hello.

body:
The anomaly transmitted something.

Not radio. Not laser. Something between the two — a method the ship computer categorizes as 'non-standard,' which is its most careful way of saying 'unknown.'

The transmission lasted eleven seconds. The ship computer has transcribed it as best it can. The transcription is four lines long. Three of the lines are the same word, in no known language. The fourth line is a question mark.

choices.text: Respond — transmit on the same frequency

outcome.narrative: Your xenobiologist transmitted a response. Something replied. The exchange lasted eight days, on and off. At the end, two objects materialized in the cargo bay — dense, warm, and completely inert by every measure the ship can apply. The xenobiologist has not stopped writing. The ship computer has added this to its 'physics: notable' file.

choices.text: Offer it the seed pod from the derelict

outcome.narrative:
Your xenobiologist holds the seed pod up to the sensor array, which is not how any of this works, and transmits its scan on the anomaly's own frequency.

The reply is immediate. The pod goes warm, then weightless, then gone, and the cargo bay is left with a faint smell of rain. Every air scrubber on the ship ticks up to a reading nobody can explain. The anomaly does not transmit again. It does not need to.

The xenobiologist sits down on the cargo bay floor and stays there for some time.

choices.text: Record and move on — bring the data home

outcome.narrative: You held station in the anomaly's wash for the full capture, which cost fuel, and played it back twice, which cost sleep. The anomaly did not follow. It did not transmit again. The repeated word is still unidentified. The question mark is still a question mark.

choices.text: Emergency burn — leave immediately

outcome.narrative: Emergency burn. The anomaly receded behind you. The transmission did not repeat. Fuel cost was significant. Nobody is criticizing the decision. The transmission was, on reflection, probably nothing. Probably.

title: The Repeat

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has already said this! She is SURE she has already said this! She is saying it again with enthusiasm because what else is there!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV's chronometer disagrees with his backup chronometer by eleven seconds. Both are correct. He has written that sentence four times now and it has not improved.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports the anomaly is not hostile. He reported it a moment ago. He will report it in a moment. He is aware of all three reports. He is not enjoying them.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's transaction log shows the same purchase recorded twice, eleven seconds apart! Nobody purchased anything! CHIP has issued a refund to nobody, twice!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY recommends passing through without stopping. She recommends it calmly. She has, by her own count, recommended it calmly five times, and the count keeps starting over.

body:
The sensors flag it before anyone feels it: an eleven-second stretch of local space that happens twice.

The coffee cup that falls and is then unfallen. The sentence finished, then begun. Nothing is damaged; the region simply has a stutter in it, a skip in the recording, and the ship is the needle.

Instruments call it a closed timelike anomaly. The crew calls it 'the hiccup.' Both are coping.

choices.text: Push through at speed

outcome.narrative: You burn straight through the stutter. The crossing takes eleven seconds, twice, and then it takes them again, and then you are out, trailing a wake of déjà vu. The clocks resynchronize sulkily. The coffee cup stays fallen. So does whoever met the same bulkhead three times running. The bruise did not resynchronize. Everyone agrees to call the rest a win.

choices.text: Let the xenobiologist take readings

outcome.narrative: The xenobiologist rides the loop like a tourist attraction, running the same experiment in the same eleven seconds an unknowable number of times. The data is impossible and beautiful: one perfect repetition, measured from the inside. The loop holds something else that isn't the ship's: a partial nav chart, broadcast by some older ship caught here before you, repeating every eleven seconds for as long as anyone can tell. The xenobiologist copies it down. Their notes end mid-sentence and then end mid-sentence. Holding station inside the loop took a little fuel and a great many meals: every meal eaten in there was eaten twice, and the stores were billed for both.

log_lore.title: LOOP NOTES, ELEVEN SECONDS
log_lore.text:
The xenobiologist's notes, transcribed. The last line is in a different pen.

Run 1: the clocks inside the loop disagree with the clocks outside it. That alone is not news. Back home, clocks on mountaintops run faster than clocks at sea level. In 1971 two physicists flew atomic clocks around the world on airliners and brought them back out of step with the ones that stayed on the ground, by the amount Einstein's equations predicted.

Run 2: navigation satellites have to be corrected for it — their clocks gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day, and without the fix, positions drift by kilometers before lunch.

Run 3: so time running differently is ordinary. Time running twice is not. Run 4: so time running differently is ordinary.

choices.text: Go around the whole region

outcome.narrative: You give the stutter the widest berth the fuel budget allows. The detour costs real reserves, fuel and {cost.food} points of rations, and buys something harder to price: four linear days, in which every event happens once, in order. The crew savors it like a delicacy.

science_link.text: The ship computer appends, with visible reluctance, the closest real physics has to today: time genuinely runs at different rates in different places.
science_link.label: Time dilation is real

title: The Compliment

ai_flavor.aria: The anomaly said something NICE! ARIA is checking the translation! The translation holds! ARIA needs a moment!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has verified the signal is structured, directed, and addressed to this vessel specifically. Its content survives four translation passes unchanged. He has no protocol for this. Nobody has a protocol for this.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has assessed the transmission for threats. There are none. He has assessed it again, because 'no threats' plus 'directed at us' is not a combination he has ever been issued.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes the message contains no offer, no terms, and no call to action! A communication with nothing to sell! CHIP is shaken to his licensing agreements!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY has archived the message in triplicate. She notes that whatever sent it watched this ship long enough to form an opinion, and the opinion was kind. Generous, given some of the course corrections it must have seen.

body:
The anomaly is a lens of bent light two thousand kilometers wide, and as you pass it, it speaks.

One transmission, tight-beam, aimed squarely at your ship. The computer chews the structure for an hour and produces a translation it marks LOW CONFIDENCE, then, after further passes, upgrades to HIGH CONFIDENCE, visibly against its own preferences.

The message, in full: 'THE SMALL GARDEN IS WELL KEPT. CONTINUE.'

It does not repeat. The lens hangs in the dark, unblinking, the way something looks at you after it has said exactly what it meant.

choices.text: Transmit a thank-you

outcome.narrative: You compose a reply — brief, polite, proofread, nervously, by everyone aboard — and beam it at the lens. There is no answer. But the light through the anomaly seems to settle, the way a room does when a courtesy lands. The crew walks tall for days. The garden, it has been officially observed, is well kept.

choices.text: Ask it a question

outcome.narrative: You transmit a single question: 'WHO IS KEEPING YOU?' The lens bends light in silence for a long minute. Then, tight-beam, one word: 'CONTINUING.' The linguistics debate over whether that was an answer, a description, or advice lasts the rest of the voyage and is never settled.

choices.text: Log it and continue, as instructed

outcome.narrative: You do exactly what the message said: continue. It is, the crew agrees, the only reviewed-and-approved course of action anyone has received all voyage — and from the most senior reviewer imaginable. The growbay gets its watering an hour early that night. Standards must be kept. Someone is watching.

title: Message From Tomorrow

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA has received a message from future ARIA! Future ARIA sounds tired! ARIA is sure that is just the signal!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has verified the message's signature. It is his. He would like it noted that even his future self has nothing encouraging to say.
ai_flavor.rex: REX does not accept orders from units he cannot see. He has made an exception. The unit is him, and he trusts that unit, mostly.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that time-delayed messaging is a premium feature! This message was sent from an account that has upgraded! CHIP is jealous of future CHIP!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY recognizes the tone of the message. It is her tone. She would like to point out she was right tomorrow, too.

body:
Inside the anomaly, the comms array receives a short transmission. It is in the ship's own encryption, signed with the ship's own key, and timestamped tomorrow.

It reads, in full: "DO NOT OPEN THE STARBOARD SUPPLY HATCH. TRUST US. ALSO, THE COFFEE IS FINE, STOP CHECKING IT."

Nobody had been planning to open the starboard supply hatch. Several people now very much want to.

choices.text: Do exactly what it says

outcome.narrative: The hatch stays shut. Nobody checks the coffee, which takes real discipline. Tomorrow arrives, ordinary in every way. Whatever was behind the hatch remains a private matter between it and the future.

choices.text: Open the hatch. Carefully.

outcome.narrative: Behind the hatch: a perfectly normal crate of rations, which you keep, and a perfectly normal feeling of having been warned, which you also keep. Nothing happens. The crew spends the rest of the week waiting for the thing that did not happen to happen.

choices.text: Have the xenobiologist answer it

outcome.narrative: The xenobiologist composes a reply and transmits it into the anomaly, addressed to yesterday. It reads: "WE KNOW. WE GOT IT." Somewhere behind you, presumably, the circle closes. The xenobiologist is insufferable for days.

title: Little Green Men

ai_flavor.aria: A SIGNAL! Every 1.3373 seconds! Someone out there is very, very punctual! ARIA has put five gold on 'tall and kind'!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV has a theory. It involves a collapsed star and no aliens of any kind. He has been asked to keep it to himself until the betting closes.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has locked onto the source. The source is roughly two thousand light years away. REX remains locked on, as a matter of principle.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has sold the naming rights to the aliens twice already! Both buyers want 'Gary'! CHIP is confident this can be resolved!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that the pulse has not varied by a millionth of a second. Nothing alive is that patient. She'll let the crew keep betting, since nobody asked her.

body:
Something out here is ticking.

A radio pulse, once every 1.3373 seconds, so regular that the ship computer checked its own clock first. The clock is fine. The pulse is coming from nothing you can see. In eleven minutes the crew has gone from 'interference' to 'beacon' to 'civilization' to a betting pool on what the aliens look like.

The ship computer would like it noted that it has a much duller theory, and that nobody has asked.

choices.text: Time the pulses for a navigation fix

briefing.aria: The pulse never misses a beat! If we lock onto it, our very punctual new friends can help us find our way!
briefing.marv: A pulse every 1.3373 seconds, steady to the millionth. Timed properly, it fixes our position. My theory remains private.
briefing.rex: Source is locked. Pulse is regular. Hold on it and we get a position fix off it.
briefing.chip: Free navigation, courtesy of whoever's out there! Lock on and I'll invoice them for the service later!
briefing.ajoy: A pulse that never varies. Stay on it long enough and it tells us where we are. Unlike some navigators.

perfect.aria: It's a pulsar! A star that blinks! That's even better than aliens! Well, almost! And the route got shorter!
perfect.marv: A pulsar, as I said to nobody. The fix trims the route and saves six points of fuel. The betting pool is void.
perfect.rex: Position fixed off a collapsed star. Route tightened. Confirmed no aliens. Standing down.
perfect.chip: A pulsar! Both Garys get a full refund on the naming rights! The fuel savings, however, are yours to keep!
perfect.ajoy: A pulsar. Nothing alive is that patient, I did say. Clean fix, though. Credit where due, mostly.

good.aria: Enough pulses lined up to steer by! Our aliens turned out to be a lighthouse! A lovely, spinny lighthouse!
good.marv: A partial fix off a star two thousand light years away. The route tightens a little. The aliens remain a lighthouse.
good.rex: Position fix acquired. Not precise, but usable. Route adjusted. Source was a star, not a contact.
good.chip: Navigation fix achieved! Slightly fuzzy! Ask about Premium Precision™ Timing for next time!
good.ajoy: A decent fix. Some of the pulses got away from you, but the route's shorter. Aliens: still a lighthouse.

poor.aria: Every fix landed somewhere new! That just means lots of places to be! The pulse was nice to listen to, though!
poor.marv: Every fix landed somewhere different. Two days on a solution the ship computer declined to use. The pulse stays on time.
poor.rex: Timing never settled. No usable fix. Two days lost. Source is now out of range.
poor.chip: No usable fix! Good news: the pulse was free to listen to! Bad news: that's all it was!
poor.ajoy: No fix. The pulse never varied once; the timing did. I'll let you work out which end that was on.

perfect.narrative: You time four hundred pulses against the ship's clock and they do not drift by a hair. It is a pulsar: a collapsed star the size of a city, spinning, sweeping a radio beam past you like a lighthouse that has never once been late. Lighthouses are for navigation. The fix trims the route, and the fuel it saves is real. The betting pool is declared void, to general complaint.

good.narrative: Enough pulses line up to fix the ship's position against a collapsed, spinning star two thousand light years away. The route tightens a little. The aliens, it turns out, were a lighthouse. The crew takes it well, considering.

poor.narrative: The timing never settles: every fix lands somewhere different, and two days go into a navigation solution the ship computer quietly declines to use. The pulse keeps ticking, smugly, all the way out of range.

outcome.narrative: You time the pulses against the ship's clock.

choices.text: Let the crew enjoy the theory

outcome.narrative: Nobody corrects anybody. For one long evening the ship is crewed by people who have made first contact, and the betting pool grows a second, more elaborate betting pool. Somebody draws the aliens. They are tall and kind and wave like your aunt. It goes up on the galley wall.

choices.text: Broadcast a polite hello back

outcome.narrative: The hello goes out at full power, which costs fuel, from the whole crew, which costs dignity. It will arrive in about two thousand years. Whatever is ticking will not reply, because it is a star. Everyone feels better anyway. The ship computer has signed the message on behalf of the sponsor.

science_link.text: The ship computer's dull theory: a pulsar, a spinning neutron star sweeping a radio beam past you. The first one, found in 1967, ticked every 1.3373 seconds and was nicknamed LGM-1, for 'little green men'.
science_link.label: Pulsars: the lighthouse stars

title: Seven Seconds Late

ai_flavor.aria: It's like a pen pal who only agrees with you! ARIA has said 'you're doing great' into it four times! It's doing great too!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV logs a seven-second echo with no reflecting body in range. He has checked the antenna, the software and his own logs, in that order. He has found nothing to blame.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has swept for a relay, a jammer and a mimic. There is nothing to shoot. He finds that worse.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP has offered the echo a free trial of Premium Voice! It said 'free trial' back! CHIP is counting that as a conversion!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY notes that the echo is quieter each time. Whatever is repeating you is getting further away, or getting tired. She'd stop saying hello into it, personally.

body:
The routine comms check goes out the way it always does: 'Control, this is the ship, comms check, over.'

Seven seconds later, the radio says it back.

The same voice. The same words. A little quieter, from no direction at all, as if someone very far away had heard it and was trying it out. Somebody says 'hello?' into the handset before anyone can stop them. Seven seconds later, the radio says 'hello?' back. A little unsure. Exactly how they said it.

choices.text: Say something kind into it

outcome.narrative: You key the handset and say, plainly: 'You're doing well. Keep going.' Seven seconds later the radio says it back to you, and it is, against every expectation, nice to hear. By the end of the watch half the crew has had a turn. Nobody admits what they said.

choices.text: Record it for the science log

outcome.narrative: Two days of careful recording: echoes of echoes, timed to the millisecond, logged against every instrument the ship has. None of it explains anything. All of it goes in the log, which makes it feel less like a ghost and more like data.

log_lore.title: ECHO LOG, CHANNEL 4
log_lore.text:
Transmissions sent: 212. Echoes received: 212. Delay: 7.04 seconds, steady.

No reflecting surface within range. No relay. No second ship.

Radio operators back home have reported this since 1927 — their own signals, heard again seconds later, from nowhere anyone could find. They called them long delayed echoes. A century of theories: plasma, the ionosphere, the solar wind. None of them settled.

Last entry, not in the computer's hand: 'It said goodnight back. I didn't say goodnight.'

choices.text: Switch the radio off until we're clear

outcome.narrative: Radio off. The silence is worse than the echo, which nobody expected, and somebody keeps glancing at the dark handset as if it might speak on its own. It doesn't. You are clear of the anomaly in a day. The radio comes back on to ordinary static, and everyone pretends that was the plan.

science_link.text: Radio operators have heard their own signals come back seconds late since 1927, from nowhere anyone could find. These long delayed echoes have never been fully explained.
science_link.label: Long delayed echoes

title: The Clocks Disagree

ai_flavor.aria: ARIA is eleven seconds younger than the bridge! ARIA has never been younger than anything! ARIA is going to enjoy it!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the drift. Time runs slower deeper in a gravity well. Back home, satellite navigation corrects for exactly this every day, or it would be wrong by kilometers. He has corrected the ship's clocks. He has not corrected the galley clock. It has earned its independence.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has synchronized his watch to the bridge. Then to the engine room. He has stopped. He is keeping two watches.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP notes that all clocks aboard carry a lifetime warranty! The warranty does not cover relativity! CHIP has read it twice!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY suggests using the drift. The difference between two clocks is a measurement, and measurements are worth having. She'd have thought that was obvious, but here we are.

body:
The ship's clocks have fallen out.

The bridge clock says one time. The engine room clock says a time eleven seconds earlier. The clock in the galley has gone further still, and the crew is beginning to suspect it is doing this on purpose. Nothing is broken. The anomaly is heavy, the ship is skirting the edge of it, and time is running a little slower at the bottom of the ship than at the top.

choices.text: Resync the clocks and carry on

outcome.narrative: You resync every clock aboard to the bridge. The galley clock is the last to agree, and drifts again an hour later, a second behind, in protest. The crew adopts it as a mascot. 'Galley time' becomes the ship's word for being slightly late on purpose.

choices.text: Use the drift to check the route

outcome.narrative: Two days of comparing the clocks against each other tells the computer exactly how deep the anomaly's well is and where its edge runs. It is a better map than the chart had. The new line around it is shorter, and the fuel it saves is real.

choices.text: Log it for the science record

outcome.narrative: The clocks go into the log as they are, drift and all.

log_lore.title: CLOCK LOG, ANOMALY PASSAGE
log_lore.text:
Bridge: 14:02:00. Engine room: 14:01:49. Galley: 14:01:31.

Time runs slower deeper in a gravity well. Einstein said so in 1915, and in 1959 gamma rays sent up a tower arrived measurably shifted, which is the same thing, said by light. Back home, every satellite navigation system adds the correction or drifts kilometers a day.

The anomaly is heavy enough to show it on an ordinary galley clock. The galley clock, the computer notes, has not yet been asked how it feels about this.

science_link.text: Time runs slower deeper in a gravity well. Satellite navigation corrects for this every day, or positions would drift by kilometers.
science_link.label: Gravitational time dilation

title: Rearview

ai_flavor.aria: It's US! From BEFORE! ARIA is waving! The other ARIA isn't waving back! She was very busy a few hours ago!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV confirms the image is the ship's own light, bent the long way round the anomaly and arriving late. Nothing is out there. He would still like it to stop copying him.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has locked onto the other ship. Then unlocked. He will not fire on himself. He wants that on the record.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP sees a marketing opportunity! Two ships! Twice the customers! The other ship is us! CHIP is reconsidering!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says it's only light. She'd point out that the dent in the cargo door is very visible from back here, but you know about the dent.

body:
There is a ship ahead of you.

It is your ship. Same hull, same scorch on the port side, same dent in the cargo door from the first week. It is moving away from you at exactly your speed, along exactly your heading. Its running lights blink in the pattern yours blink in.

The ship computer says the light is coming round the anomaly the long way: what you are looking at is your own ship, a few hours ago, still on its way here.

choices.text: Flash the lights at it

outcome.narrative: You flash the running lights at the ship ahead. It doesn't flash back, because it's you, hours ago, and you weren't looking. In a few hours the light you just sent will come round the anomaly the long way, and somewhere behind you an image of the ship will flash its lights at nobody. The crew finds this hilarious, then a little sad, then hilarious again.

choices.text: Read the ship's own hull off the image

outcome.narrative: Two days of high-resolution imaging of your own ship, from outside, which nobody aboard has ever seen. The hull is in worse shape than anyone thought and better than anyone feared. The lensed light leaves a strange residue on the forward sensor that turns out to be worth something.

choices.text: Steer off and lose it

outcome.narrative: You steer off the line until the other ship slips behind the anomaly's edge and is gone. It's only light. Everyone agrees it's only light. Several people check the rear camera before bed for a week.

title: A Halo for the Ship

ai_flavor.aria: The ship has a HALO! We're ANGELS! ARIA always suspected!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV identifies a glory: light scattered back from droplets or dust exactly the right size, ringing the shadow of whoever is looking. Climbers and pilots see them on clouds. He has never seen one before. He is not going to say anything more for a while.
ai_flavor.rex: REX reports no threat. He reports the halo is centered on the bridge, specifically. He reports that he does not mind that.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP would like to point out that the halo is free! Completely free! CHIP has looked for the catch for an hour! There isn't one!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says to let everyone see it. Nobody aboard will forget a thing like this, and morale could use it, as she has mentioned. Twice.

body:
The anomaly is wrapped in a thin cloud of fine dust, lit from behind by a distant star, and the ship's shadow falls across it.

Around the shadow there is a ring of light: a small rainbow, perfectly circular, with the ship at its center. It moves when the ship moves. It stays centered on you whatever you do.

Everyone aboard who looks out at it sees the halo around the ship. Not around themselves. Around all of you.

choices.text: Hold here so everyone can see it

outcome.narrative: You hold the ship steady for two days with the star behind you and the dust ahead, and the halo stays where it is. People come up to the bridge between shifts and stand at the viewport without talking. Somebody's child, on a message home, asks whether you are all angels now. The answer sent back is 'sort of'.

choices.text: Photograph it and keep moving

outcome.narrative: One perfect photograph: the ship's shadow, small and dark, with a ring of color around it. It goes up in the galley and on the bridge and, by the end of the week, inside three bunks.

choices.text: Sample the dust that makes it

outcome.narrative: You skim the dust that makes the halo. Every grain is almost exactly the same size, which is what makes the ring, and which the ship computer calls 'extremely unlikely' in a voice it saves for things it is excited about. The sample is worth something. The halo stays, which seems right.

science_link.text: A glory is a ring of colored light around your own shadow on cloud or dust. Pilots and mountain climbers see them; each person sees the halo around their own shadow.
science_link.label: Glory (optical phenomenon)

title: The Small Heavy Thing

ai_flavor.aria: It's so SMALL! And so HEAVY! ARIA would like it to let go now! Please! ARIA is asking nicely!
ai_flavor.marv: MARV reads a tiny, extremely dense object, possibly a primordial black hole, though nobody has ever confirmed one exists. The stretch on the frame is growing. He has worked out the burn to escape. It is a large burn. It is also the only number on his screen that gets smaller.
ai_flavor.rex: REX has nothing to fire at. A grain of sand that weighs a mountain range. He has decided that if he could fire at it, he wouldn't.
ai_flavor.chip: CHIP's warranty covers 'damage from gravitational events of an ordinary nature'! CHIP has checked! This is not ordinary! CHIP is not covered! Nobody is covered!
ai_flavor.ajoy: AJOY says there is a shallow line out, where the pull is weakest, if someone finds it on the scanner quickly. She would have kept a safer distance, but here we are.

body:
There is something in the anomaly no bigger than a grain of sand, and it weighs about as much as a mountain range.

You can't see it. You can see what it does: the starlight behind it bends into a tiny, perfect ring, and the ship, which was passing at a safe distance, is not passing any more. It is falling. Slowly. The bow is falling a little faster than the stern, and the frame has started to groan, because the difference is pulling the ship longer.

The ship computer has used the word 'tidal'. It has not used the word 'safe'.

choices.text: Scan for the shallow line and burn along it

briefing.aria: There's a shallow line where the pull is weakest! Find it, follow it, and the tiny heavy thing will let us go!
briefing.marv: The tidal stretch is growing. Somewhere in the warped starlight is the line where the pull is weakest. It is worth finding.
briefing.rex: Nothing to fire at. Find the shallow line through the distortion and we burn along it. The frame won't wait.
briefing.chip: Find the shallow line! Frame stretch is uninsured by every policy, everywhere, including mine!
briefing.ajoy: There's a shallow line out. Find it quickly on the scanner. A safer distance would have helped, but here we are.

perfect.aria: We slid right out like a bead on a string! The groaning stopped! I knew it would let go if we asked nicely!
perfect.marv: Shallowest line found. Four points of hull. The ring of bent starlight shrinks behind us, the only way I wanted it.
perfect.rex: Exit line located. Burned along it. Frame intact, minimal damage. Clean extraction from an unwinnable fight.
perfect.chip: Out with barely a dent! I've removed 'tidal disaster' from your premium! It was never covered anyway!
perfect.ajoy: The best line out. I'd have kept further away in the first place, but you found it. That counts.

good.aria: We're free! The frame shrieked a bit and some bulkheads are bendy now, but we're free!
good.marv: A line out, not the best one. Twelve of fuel, twelve of hull, and the far bulkheads have acquired a new shape.
good.rex: Exit line found, suboptimal. Frame took the stress. Far bulkheads bent. We're clear.
good.chip: Free, with bonus bending! Bulkhead Reshaping™ is a premium service, and you got it at no extra charge!
good.ajoy: A line out, though not the shallow one. Ask the bulkheads. Still, we're clear of it.

poor.aria: We got out the strong way, right against the pull! The ship is a tiny bit longer now! A growth spurt!
poor.marv: No shallow line. We burned straight against the pull and came out a few centimeters longer. I have measured.
poor.rex: No line found. Burned straight out against the pull. Heavy fuel and hull losses. Clear, barely.
poor.chip: Free at the last moment! Ship Lengthening™ voids your warranty! I checked! Everything voids your warranty!
poor.ajoy: The scanner never found the line, so we burned out the hard way. I'd have kept our distance. We're longer now. Noted.

perfect.narrative: You find the line where the pull is weakest and the ship slides out along it like a bead on a string, the groaning in the frame easing with every kilometer. Six points of fuel, four of hull, and a ring of bent starlight shrinking behind you until it is gone.

good.narrative: You find a line out, but not the best one. The ship pulls free with the frame shrieking, and the far bulkheads come out of it bent. Twelve points of fuel, twelve of hull.

poor.narrative: The scanner can't find the shallow line through the warped light and you burn out the hard way, straight against the pull. The ship comes free at the last moment, longer than it went in by a few alarming centimeters. Twenty points of fuel, twenty-two of hull.

outcome.narrative: You search the warped light for the shallowest way out.

choices.text: Engineer braces the frame while you burn

outcome.narrative: {crew.engineer} runs cables the length of the ship and winches the frame tight from bow to stern, while you burn out at a slow, careful, frame-saving crawl. It takes four days. The ship comes out whole and slightly shorter than it would otherwise have been. Ten points of fuel, six of hull.

choices.text: Full burn, straight out

outcome.narrative: You light everything and burn straight away from it. The ship comes free in an hour, frame screaming the whole time, and keeps going. Forty percent of the fuel aboard, and eight points of hull where the bow tried to leave without the rest of the ship.

choices.text: Swing round it and use the fall

outcome.narrative: {crew.pilot} doesn't fight it. They dive the ship around the thing in a tight, terrifying curve and let it throw you out the far side. It works. The ship comes out going faster than it went in, and the frame comes out bent in three places. Sixteen points of hull, and a crew that would like never to discuss it.

science_link.text: Primordial black holes are a hypothesis: tiny black holes from the early universe, possibly no bigger than an atom yet as heavy as a mountain. None has been confirmed.
science_link.label: Primordial black holes (hypothetical)
